pages.guide: Component Guide Human View Machine View Overview Add-on is a single-line text field with a fixed, non-editable prefix and/or suffix segment attached directly to it - used when the value alone would be ambiguous or would force the user to retype a constant part of it every time. When to Use A value with a fixed protocol or domain prefix - https:// before a URL. A currency symbol on a price - $ before a numeric amount. A username handle with a fixed platform prefix - @ before a handle, or a fixed email domain suffix. When Not to Use A value with no natural constant part - use a plain Input - adding an empty or irrelevant add-on segment is just visual noise. A prefix/suffix that the user should be able to edit or choose - use a Select alongside the field, or a Group Button, instead of a fixed, non-editable add-on. Multiple independent constant parts on both sides that combine in complex ways - consider breaking the field into clearly labeled separate inputs instead. Best Practices Keep the add-on segment visually distinct but clearly non-editable (different background, no cursor) so users don't try to click into it. Use the add-on only for a genuinely constant part of the value - never for something that varies per use case. Make sure the combined value (prefix + typed value + suffix) is what actually gets submitted, not just displayed. Do and Don't Do Price£per month The add-ons carry the unit, so the input holds only the number the user actually has to type. Don't PriceSet the amount An add-on used as a label steals the width the value needs and leaves the field itself unlabelled. Add-ons are for units and fixed fragments, not instructions. Accessibility The prefix/suffix text is exposed to assistive technology alongside the field's label, so its meaning isn't lost for screen-reader users. The editable portion remains a real, independently focusable input - the add-on segments are not part of the tab order since they aren't interactive. Sufficient contrast between the add-on segment and the editable field, so the boundary between fixed and editable text is visually clear. pages.guide: Component Guide Human View Machine View Overview Affix pins an element to the viewport once the page scrolls past its original position, so it stays reachable - distinct from Float Button, which is always corner-anchored regardless of scroll, and distinct from Header/Modal overlays, which aren't tied to scroll position at all. When to Use A filter or toolbar above a long list or table - stays available without scrolling back up. A table's header row - column labels stay visible while scrolling through many rows. A persistent call-to-action or a section sub-navigation - anything that should remain reachable throughout a long page. When Not to Use A single, always-corner-anchored action unrelated to scroll position - use Float Button instead. Short pages with no meaningful scroll distance - affixing adds complexity with no real benefit if the whole page already fits in view. Elements that must stay in a fixed spot regardless of any particular trigger point - use a real fixed-position layout element instead of Affix's scroll-triggered pinning. Best Practices Keep the affixed element visually distinct once pinned (a subtle shadow or border) so users notice it detached from the page flow. Affix only content that benefits from constant visibility - overusing it on multiple elements at once creates a cluttered, competing set of sticky bars. Account for the affixed element's height when it overlaps content below it, so nothing gets permanently hidden underneath it. Do and Don't Do StickySave bar - pins once its normal position scrolls out of view Pins a short, persistently-useful action bar, and only once the page has scrolled past where it would normally sit. Don't StickyFull article text - pinned for the entire length of the page Pinning a large block of content for the whole scroll permanently eats screen space the reader needs for the content moving underneath it. Accessibility The affixed element keeps its place in the reading/tab order - affixing is a purely visual position change, not a DOM reordering. Sufficient contrast and a visible boundary (shadow/border) once affixed, so it doesn't visually blend into whatever scrolls beneath it. Never affix content that would then overlap and obscure keyboard focus elsewhere on the page. pages.guide: Component Guide Human View Machine View Overview Alert surfaces a status message inline within page content, like "Your changes have been saved." - it sits flush in the normal page flow, full width of its container, unlike Toast which floats above the page in a fixed corner. When to Use A save or action confirmation embedded in the page - "Your changes have been saved." System status or a maintenance notice - a persistent banner that stays until dismissed or resolved. A form-level validation summary - listing every error at the top of a form. When Not to Use A temporary confirmation that shouldn't require the user to stay on the page - use Toast, which floats and self-dismisses. A message that must block interaction until acknowledged - use Modal - Alert never interrupts the page, it just sits within it. A short hint tied to a specific control - use Tooltip instead of a full-width banner for a small, localized hint. Best Practices Match the type (info/success/warning/error) to the actual severity - overusing error styling for minor notices trains users to ignore it. Keep the message specific and actionable ("Your card expired - update payment details"), not a vague "Something happened." Only make it dismissible when the information genuinely stops being relevant after being read once. Do and Don't Do Card expiredUpdate your payment details to avoid interruption. Names what happened and what to do about it, so the message is actionable on its own. Don't ErrorSomething went wrong. Tells the user only that they are stuck. With no cause and no next step, the alert costs attention and returns nothing. Accessibility role="alert" is not universal here - it belongs only on an Alert that is dynamically inserted in response to something, such as "3 validation errors" appearing after a failed form submit, where the assertive announcement is the point. The Alert shown in the Live Preview and in the Do/Don't demos above is static markup, present when the page renders rather than injected afterward, so it intentionally carries no role="alert" here - adding one would fire a disruptive assistive-technology announcement every time the page loads, which is a real anti-pattern, not a safe default to copy onto every Alert. When an Alert genuinely is inserted dynamically, use role="alert" (assertive) for errors that need immediate attention, or role="status" (polite) for a lower-urgency dynamic update - and apply it in code at the point of insertion, not as a permanent attribute on a banner that's simply always there. Type is communicated by an icon and text, not color alone, for users with color-vision deficiencies. The dismiss control (when present) has an accessible name ("Dismiss this alert"), not just an X icon. pages.guide: Component Guide Human View Machine View Overview Anchor is plain inline navigational text, like "Learn more" or "View documentation", used for wayfinding within copy, lists, and footers - distinct from Button's boxed Link type, which reads as a call-to-action rather than a piece of body text. When to Use A read-more or view-details link inside body copy - sitting naturally within a sentence or paragraph. An external reference or citation - linking out to a source. Inline documentation or footer navigation links - a list of plain text links with no boxed emphasis. When Not to Use An action that needs to stand out among other buttons - use Button's Link type instead, which is built to sit inside a button row. A call to action that should draw attention - use Primary or Secondary Button - Anchor is intentionally understated. A non-navigational action (submitting, deleting, toggling something) - Anchor implies going somewhere; use a real Button for actions that aren't navigation. Best Practices Use descriptive link text ("View pricing", not "Click here"), since link text alone should make sense out of context. Keep its styling consistent everywhere it appears, so users learn to recognize it as a link at a glance. Reserve the icon-trailing variant for links that genuinely leave the current context (external sites, downloads). Do and Don't Do OverviewPricingFAQ The section currently in view is visually distinct, so Anchor doubles as a reading progress indicator, not just a list of jump links. Don't OverviewPricingFAQ With no active state, Anchor is just a table of contents that cannot tell the reader where they already are on a long page. Accessibility Renders as a real link when it navigates, so screen readers announce it correctly and it's included in link-only navigation. Visited and focus states are visually distinct, never color-only, from the rest state. An external-link icon is paired with descriptive text or an accessible label noting it opens externally. pages.guide: Component Guide Human View Machine View Overview Autocomplete is a text field that shows a live list of matching suggestions as the user types, while still accepting a free-form value the user keeps typing past the suggestions - a hybrid between Input's free text and Select's closed option list. When to Use A search-like field with known likely values - a city search, a product lookup. Picking from a large option set faster by typing - a tag picker, a contact search. A command or query input - where suggestions speed up entry but a fully custom value is still valid. When Not to Use The value must be one of a small, fixed set with no free text allowed - use Select instead so an invalid value can't be submitted. There's no meaningful suggestion source - a plain Input is simpler when there's nothing useful to suggest. Hierarchical, drill-down data - use Cascader or Tree Select rather than a flat suggestion list. Best Practices Debounce suggestion lookups so fast typing doesn't spam a search on every keystroke. Highlight the matched portion of each suggestion so it's clear why it appeared. Always allow submitting the typed value even if the user never selects a suggestion, unless the field truly requires a match. Do and Don't Do CityManchesterManilaMannheim A short list of real matches narrowed by what has been typed, so choosing is faster than finishing the word. Don't CityAberdeenAdelaideAlbuquerque Suggestions that ignore the query are noise the user has to read past. If nothing matches, say so instead of listing the top of the list. Accessibility Implemented with combobox semantics, so the suggestion list is announced and arrow keys move through it without leaving the input. The number of available suggestions is announced as they update, so screen-reader users know the list changed. Selecting a suggestion with Enter or click produces the same result, and Escape closes the list without clearing typed text. pages.guide: Component Guide Human View Machine View Overview Avatar represents a person throughout the product - in a profile menu, a comment, a team list, or an assignee indicator - a compact circular (or square) visual identifier shown as an image, initials, or a generic icon placeholder. When to Use A user profile menu or comment author - identifying who's associated with an action or piece of content. A team member list or an assignee indicator - showing who's involved at a glance. A chat participant list - compact identification across many people at once. When Not to Use Representing something that isn't a person or team - use Image or an icon instead - Avatar specifically implies identity. A context where a full name is more useful than a small visual - pair Avatar with a name rather than relying on the image alone when precision matters. A large, detailed profile photo display - use Image - Avatar is built for small, compact identification, not a full photo viewer. Best Practices Fall back to initials or a generic icon gracefully when no photo is available, rather than showing a broken image. Keep sizing consistent within any one context (all comments the same avatar size, for example). Use the presence/status dot sparingly and only when online/away/offline genuinely matters in that context. Do and Don't Do JD Two solid initials at a size that stays legible, with presence shown as a small status dot rather than competing text. Don't JOHNATHAN A full name crammed into a 40px circle is unreadable at any size. Avatars carry one or two initials - use a name label beside it for the rest. Accessibility Carries an accessible name identifying the person ("Jordan Lee's avatar" or simply the person's name), not left unlabeled. A presence dot's meaning (online/away/offline) is exposed in text or an accessible label, not communicated by color alone. Initials fallback text meets sufficient contrast against its background circle. pages.guide: Component Guide Human View Machine View Overview Badge draws attention to a count, a new item, or a status without interrupting the flow - a small dot, number, or short status label typically overlaid on or placed beside another element, like a notification bell or an avatar. When to Use An unread notification count - a number badge on a bell or inbox icon. A new-feature indicator dot - flagging something recently added. An account status label or a cart item count - a compact signal attached to another element. When Not to Use Standalone status text with no attached element - use Tag instead - Badge is meant to overlay or sit beside something else, not stand alone. A count so large or so central to the task that it deserves its own visible number in the main content - don't shrink primary information into a small corner badge. A persistent label describing a whole row or card's category - use Tag, which is built for that role. Best Practices Cap large counts with a "99+" style ceiling rather than letting the badge grow to fit an arbitrarily large number. Reserve badge colors consistently (e.g. red for alerts, neutral for plain counts) across the product. Remove or hide the badge entirely at zero/none, rather than showing an empty "0". Do and Don't Do ✉3 A real count on the object it belongs to, so the number means exactly one thing: unread items in that inbox. Don't Everything is fine, no action needed right now A sentence-length label defeats what a badge is for - a glance, not a read. Keep the label to a word or two, or drop it for the dot alone. Accessibility The count or status is exposed to assistive technology as text, not conveyed by a colored dot alone. pages.guide: Component Guide Human View Machine View Overview Breadcrumb is a horizontal trail of navigational links showing the user's current location within a hierarchy, separated by a divider - the last item is always the current page, shown as plain text rather than a clickable link. When to Use A product category trail - Home / Electronics / Laptops. A file or folder path - showing nested location within a file browser. Documentation hierarchy or a multi-step form's current section - anywhere retracing the path back up the hierarchy is useful. When Not to Use A flat structure with no real hierarchy - a breadcrumb implies nested depth; don't add one just to show a page title. The primary means of navigating the product - Breadcrumb supplements primary navigation (a sidebar, a nav bar) - it shouldn't be the only way to get around. A sequence of steps the user is moving through, rather than a location in a hierarchy - use Steps instead. Best Practices Keep every item except the last one a real, clickable link, so users can jump back to any ancestor level directly. Truncate very long trails (many levels deep) with an ellipsis or collapsed middle section rather than wrapping across lines - past 4 levels, show the first level, a collapsed "…" (expandable on click/tap to reveal the hidden middle levels), then the last 2 levels plus the current page. The current page (last item) is marked with aria-current="page" rather than just styled differently. pages.guide: Component Guide Human View Machine View Overview Destructive Button is a deliberately alarming, danger-colored button reserved for actions that cause irreversible consequences - deleting a record, discarding unsaved work, or canceling a subscription. Its color is the first and fastest signal a user gets that the action can't be easily undone. When to Use Deleting or permanently removing data - Delete, Remove, Terminate. Actions that discard the user's own work - Discard changes, Reset a form. Canceling something with real consequences - Cancel Subscription, Revoke access. When Not to Use Any action that is easily reversible - use Primary or Secondary instead - reserving red for real danger keeps it meaningful. As a generic "important" button - Destructive communicates risk, not priority; a merely important-but-safe action should stay Primary. Multiple destructive actions competing in the same view - surface only the one the user is actually about to take, typically behind a confirmation step. Best Practices Pair it with an explicit confirmation step (a Modal or Pop Confirm) for anything truly irreversible, rather than firing on a single click. Use a specific verb, not a bare "Yes" - "Delete project" communicates the consequence, "Yes" does not. Never use Destructive styling for a safe action just to make it stand out - it trains users to distrust the color's warning. Do and Don't Do CancelDelete project Paired with an easy way out, and used only for the one action that actually destroys something. Don't Log out Logging out is reversible in one click. Reserving red for genuinely destructive actions is what makes it trustworthy when it does appear. Accessibility Never rely on color alone to communicate danger - the label text itself should name the consequence (Delete, not just a trash icon). Same native <button> keyboard and focus behavior as every other type, with a visible focus ring in the danger color. When paired with a confirmation dialog, focus should move into that dialog so keyboard and screen-reader users aren't left on the original trigger. pages.guide: Component Guide Human View Machine View Overview Ghost Button has no fill and no border at rest, only a background or color change on hover or focus - built for toolbars, cards, and dense layouts that already provide their own visual structure, so the button doesn't need one of its own. Repeated per-item actions - row-level actions in a list or table where many buttons appear at once. Anywhere the action needs to be found at a glance - use Secondary or Tertiary if some visual weight is still needed. pages.guide: Component Guide Human View Machine View Overview The Primary Button is the highest-emphasis action in the Agentic Design System - a solid, brand-red filled button reserved for the single most important action on a screen or within a section. Its strong fill and contrast are what make it read as "the one thing to do here," so its impact depends on staying rare: a screen with more than one Primary Button no longer tells the user where to look first. When to Use The main call to action on a form or page - Save, Submit, Continue, Buy Now. The action that completes or advances a flow - Create, Generate, Start, Confirm. Exactly one per screen or logical section - a modal footer, a form, a card - never two Primary Buttons competing in the same view. Paired with a Secondary Button for the alternate action - e.g. "Save" (Primary) next to "Cancel" (Secondary). When Not to Use Supporting or optional actions - use Secondary or Tertiary instead, so the visual hierarchy still points at the real primary action. Irreversible or data-loss actions - use the Destructive type so risk is communicated by color, not just position. Plain navigation or wayfinding - use Anchor (inline text link) or Link-type Button instead of a boxed, high-emphasis button. Repeated per-row actions in a table or list - a Primary Button repeated many times in a view dilutes its meaning; use Ghost or Tertiary for row-level actions. Best Practices Keep the label a specific verb or verb phrase ("Save changes", not "OK" or "Submit" in isolation) so the action is unambiguous out of context. Place it in a predictable, consistent position (e.g. bottom-right of a modal/form footer) so users build muscle memory across the product. Never rely on color alone to convey the Disabled state - it also loses interactivity (cursor, pointer-events) and drops opacity. Don't change a Primary Button's color per screen to "match a theme" - the brand-red fill is what signals primacy; recoloring it breaks that signal everywhere else it's used correctly. Do and Don't Do Save changesCancel One Primary carrying the main action, paired with a Secondary for the alternative. The eye lands on the important one immediately. Don't SaveExportShare Three Primaries compete, so none of them reads as primary. Once everything is emphasised, nothing is. Accessibility Renders as a real <button> element, so it's reachable by keyboard (Tab) and activates with Enter/Space by default - no extra ARIA role needed. Focus state uses a visible 2px outline, never a color-only change, so keyboard users can always tell which control is focused. Text and icon colors meet WCAG 2.2 AA contrast against the red fill in both light and dark theme. Disabled buttons use the native disabled attribute (removed from the tab order and announced as unavailable by screen readers), not just a visual dim. Minimum touch target is 40px (Medium size) or larger, meeting WCAG 2.2's target-size guidance for pointer input. pages.guide: Component Guide Human View Machine View Overview Secondary Button is the supporting-action counterpart to Primary - an outlined, unfilled button used for the alternate or less urgent action in the same view, most often placed directly beside a Primary Button. When to Use The alternate action next to a Primary Button - Cancel beside Save, Back beside Continue. Actions that matter but aren't the main goal of the screen - Preview, Edit, Export, View Details. Anywhere a bordered, medium-emphasis button reads better than a full fill - toolbars, card footers, dialog footers. When Not to Use The single most important action on the screen - use Primary instead, so there is still exactly one highest-emphasis control. Irreversible actions - use Destructive so danger is communicated by color as well as position. Dense, repeated row actions - use Ghost or Tertiary, since Secondary's border still carries meaningful visual weight at scale. Best Practices Pair it with a Primary Button rather than using it alone as a screen's only action. Keep its border and label weight consistent everywhere it's the "other" choice, so users learn what a bordered button means across the product. Avoid placing two Secondary buttons side by side for genuinely different actions - if neither is more important, consider Tertiary or Ghost instead. Do and Don't Do PublishSave draft Secondary sits beside one Primary, offering a real alternative without competing for the first glance. Don't Delete account A Secondary carrying a destructive, high-stakes action undersells its own consequence. Give it Destructive's weight instead. Accessibility Same native <button> semantics as Primary - keyboard reachable, Enter/Space activates it. Border and text color meet WCAG 2.2 AA contrast against the panel background in both themes. pages.guide: Component Guide Human View Machine View Overview Tertiary Button is the lowest-emphasis boxed action in the system - text-only styling with no fill and no border at rest, used for actions that should be available but never compete visually with Primary or Secondary. When to Use Low-priority actions alongside higher-emphasis buttons - Learn More, Skip, View More. Secondary navigation inside a flow - Advanced Settings, a link to an optional step. Repeated actions in a dense layout - where even Secondary's border would add too much visual noise. When Not to Use The main or supporting action of a screen - use Primary or Secondary so the hierarchy stays legible. Irreversible actions - always use Destructive, regardless of how minor the action seems. Anywhere the action needs strong discoverability - a Tertiary button can be easy to miss; use Secondary if visibility matters. Best Practices Reserve it for genuinely optional or low-stakes actions, not as a default fallback for anything without a clear priority. Still give it a real hit target and visible focus ring even though it has no border at rest. Avoid using more than one or two Tertiary buttons in the same row - it starts to read as a wall of plain text otherwise. Do and Don't Do EditView history The lowest-emphasis option in a row that already has a stronger action above it, so the hierarchy reads top to bottom. Don't Confirm purchase A Tertiary standing alone as the only way to complete a purchase is nearly invisible. The most important action on the screen needs more than a Tertiary's weight. Focus and hover states add a visible background or underline change, since the rest state alone has very little contrast to lean on. pages.guide: Component Guide Human View Machine View Overview Calendar is a full, always-visible month grid for browsing dates or scheduling - unlike Date Picker's compact trigger-and-popup pattern, Calendar stays open on the page so an entire month can be scanned, compared, and interacted with at once. When to Use A booking or scheduling view - showing availability across a full month. A content publishing calendar or attendance tracker - seeing many dates' worth of data simultaneously. Event planning overviews or a habit-tracker grid - any case where scanning the whole month matters more than a compact popup. When Not to Use Picking a single date within a form - use Date Picker's compact trigger instead of dedicating a full grid to the page. A bounded start/end pair - use Date Range. A screen with limited space where a full month grid can't be shown clearly - consider a Date Picker's popup calendar instead of a permanently visible one. Best Practices Highlight today's date clearly and consistently, so orientation within the month is immediate. Use event dots or markers sparingly - too many per day makes the grid noisy and hard to scan. Keep the first day of the week configurable to match locale or organizational convention (Sunday vs. Monday). Do and Don't Do March 2026MoTuWeThFrSaSu29123 Leading days from the previous month are shown dimmed rather than hidden, so the grid never looks like a broken week with cells missing. Don't March 2026MoTuWe123 Starting the grid at day 1 with no leading blanks makes every week after the first misalign with its weekday header. Accessibility Each day cell is independently focusable and announces its full date, not just the day number. Today, selected, and out-of-month days are each distinguishable by more than color alone. Fully keyboard-navigable - arrow keys move between days, Page Up/Down move between months. pages.guide: Component Guide Human View Machine View Overview Card groups related content into a bordered container, with an optional cover/media area or a footer row of action buttons - a general-purpose content grouping used across dashboards, listings, and profiles wherever a distinct, self-contained unit of information needs visual containment. When to Use A dashboard summary tile - a self-contained block of related metrics or info. A product listing item or a team member profile - grouping an image, title, and details together. A settings section grouping or a blog post preview - any distinct, self-contained unit of content. When Not to Use Content that's actually a single flat list of similar rows - use List instead - wrapping every row in its own Card adds unnecessary visual weight. A small piece of contextual detail tied to a specific trigger - use Popover instead of a full Card. Structured label/value data with no need for a border or media area - use Description. Best Practices Keep one Card focused on one coherent unit of content - avoid stuffing unrelated information into the same card. Use the media/cover area only when a visual genuinely represents the card's subject, not as decoration. Keep footer actions limited to the one or two most relevant actions for that card's content. Do and Don't Do Q1 revenue reportSummary of bookings, churn and expansion for the first quarter. One subject per card, with a title short enough to scan and body copy that fits without truncating. Don't Q1 revenue report, churn analysis, and next quarter's hiring planEverything from this quarter and some notes on hiring too, plus a few other things worth mentioning here. Stacking unrelated subjects into one card makes the title wrap past recognition and the card unclickable as a single unit - split it into two. Accessibility When a whole card is clickable, it's implemented as a real link or button, not a div with only a visual hover style. Heading structure inside a card follows the page's real hierarchy (an h2/h3, not just bold text) so screen-reader navigation stays meaningful. Interactive elements inside a clickable card (like a footer button) remain independently reachable and don't get swallowed by the card's own click handler. pages.guide: Component Guide Human View Machine View Overview Cascader selects hierarchical, multi-level data - like Country / State / City - through a multi-column panel where picking an option in one column reveals the next column's choices, letting the user drill down step by step to a final value. When to Use A hierarchical address or location field - Country, then State/Province, then City. A category drill-down - a top-level category narrowing into subcategories. An org chart or file-path picker - any strictly nested structure with a clear parent-to-child relationship. When Not to Use A single flat list with no hierarchy - use Select instead - Cascader's multi-column panel adds unneeded complexity for a non-nested choice. Data that's nested but the user needs to see the whole tree at once, expanding and collapsing branches freely - use Tree Select instead of Cascader's linked-column drill-down. Free-form text with a suggestion list - use Autocomplete, not a fixed hierarchical structure. Best Practices Show the full selected path in the closed trigger (e.g. "Asia / India / Mumbai"), not just the final leaf value. Keep each column's option count reasonable - if the deepest level has hundreds of items, add search/filtering within the column. Let users jump back to an earlier column to change a prior choice without restarting the whole selection. pages.guide: Component Guide Human View Machine View Overview Collapse progressively discloses long or secondary content behind a clickable header - the content stays hidden until expanded, keeping the page compact while still making the detail available on demand. When to Use An FAQ list - each question collapsed until clicked. Settings section grouping or filter panel sections - organizing a long settings page into expandable chunks. An order details breakdown or terms and conditions section - long content that most users won't need expanded by default. When Not to Use Content everyone needs to see immediately - hiding essential information behind a click adds friction; show it directly instead. A single, always-visible section with no reason to hide it - a static Card or plain section is simpler when there's no benefit to collapsing. Switching between different views of content rather than showing/hiding one section - use Tabs instead of Collapse. Best Practices Make the whole header row clickable, not just a small chevron icon, so the hit target is generous. Default the most commonly needed section open when there's a clear default, rather than collapsing everything. Animate the expand/collapse transition smoothly so content doesn't just snap in and out abruptly. Do and Don't Do Shipping detailsDelivered by courier, 2-4 business days. A header naming exactly what is inside, so opening it is a deliberate choice rather than a guess. Don't More infoDetails Two panels both titled something generic give the user no way to predict which one holds what they need - they have to open both. Accessibility The header exposes aria-expanded, reflecting whether its panel is currently open. The header is a real, keyboard-operable button, not a div with only a click handler. pages.guide: Component Guide Human View Machine View Overview Color Picker shows the currently selected color as a swatch plus its hex value, and opens a palette of preset swatch options when focused or clicked - used for any field where the user chooses or edits a color rather than typing arbitrary text. When to Use Brand color selection - picking a primary accent color for a theme. Theme customization - letting a user personalize colors in a settings panel. Assigning a color to a chart series or a label - so categories are visually distinguishable. When Not to Use A value that isn't actually a color - use Input or Select for plain text or fixed options. A fixed, non-customizable color defined by the design system itself - there's no need for a picker when the value can never change. Selecting from a very large, unconstrained color space with precise numeric control (e.g. exact RGB channel entry) as the primary use case - pair the swatch picker with a text hex input, which this component already provides, rather than building a separate numeric-only control. Best Practices Always show the current value as both a visual swatch and its hex code, since color alone can be hard to communicate precisely. Offer a curated preset palette in addition to free hex entry, so most users never need to type a hex value. Validate typed hex values immediately and fall back to the last valid color on invalid input, rather than letting the field go blank. Do and Don't Do Brand colour#FF031A The swatch is paired with the hex value, so the choice can be read, copied and checked without trusting the screen's calibration. Don't Brand colour A swatch with no value is unreadable to anyone who cannot distinguish it from the neighbouring shade, and impossible to reproduce elsewhere. Accessibility The swatch alone never conveys the selected value - the hex text is always present for anyone who can't distinguish it visually. Preset swatches in the open panel are reachable and selectable by keyboard, not just by mouse click. The field's accessible name states what the color controls ("Brand color"), not just "Color". pages.guide: Component Guide Human View Machine View Overview Date Picker is a text field with a fixed trailing calendar icon that opens a calendar panel for selecting a single date - it prevents free-form date typos and formatting inconsistencies by letting the user pick from an actual calendar instead of typing a date string by hand. When to Use Collecting a single specific date - date of birth, a booking date, a deadline. Any date that benefits from calendar context - seeing the day of the week, nearby dates, or today's position. Filtering by a single date - "show records on this date". When Not to Use A start and end date together as one pair - use Date Range instead of two separate Date Pickers. A time of day rather than a calendar date - use Time. A date the user would rather type freely in an unusual format - a plain Input may fit better for unconstrained historical or approximate dates. Best Practices Show the selected date in the field using an unambiguous, locale-appropriate format (avoid all-numeric formats that can be misread as day/month vs. month/day). Default the calendar panel to open on today or on the currently selected date, not always the current month. Disable or visually de-emphasize out-of-range dates (past dates for a future booking, for example) rather than allowing an invalid selection to be corrected after the fact. Do and Don't Do Delivery date14 Mar 2026📅Weekdays only. An unambiguous written-out month, so the date reads the same to a reader in London and one in Chicago. Don't Delivery date03/14/26📅 All-numeric dates flip meaning between locales - 03/04 is two different days depending on where the reader is. Spell the month out. Accessibility The calendar panel is reachable and fully operable by keyboard (arrow keys to move between days, Enter to select, Escape to close). The current, focused, and selected day are each visually and programmatically distinguishable, not just by color. The field's accessible name states what date is being collected (e.g. "Date of birth"), not just "Date". pages.guide: Component Guide Human View Machine View Overview Date Range collects a start and end date together as one bounded pair in a single field - a text field showing both dates with a fixed trailing calendar icon - used whenever the two dates are meaningless apart, like a trip's start and end. When to Use Trip or booking dates - start and end, considered together. A reporting period or subscription term - a bounded window with a clear start and end. An event's duration - where showing just one date without the other would be incomplete. When Not to Use Two genuinely independent dates - use two separate Date Pickers if the dates don't form one bounded range. A single date with no end boundary - use Date Picker. A numeric range rather than a date range - use Slider or two Number fields. Best Practices Show both dates together in the field so the pair reads as one value, not two. pages.guide: Component Guide Human View Machine View Overview Divider visually separates sections of content with a horizontal rule, with an optional text label breaking the line - a lightweight, low-emphasis break between related but distinct groups of content. When to Use A section separator - marking a clear boundary between two content blocks. A form group boundary or an "Or" split between two actions - e.g. "Sign in with email" / "Or" / "Continue with Google". A separator between inline items - adjacent to a Breadcrumb, or between items in a row. When Not to Use Spacing alone would already communicate the separation - don't add a visible line where whitespace is sufficient - overusing dividers adds visual clutter. A boundary that also needs to be interactive or collapsible - use Collapse instead of a plain static Divider. Separating truly unrelated content that shouldn't appear together at all - a Divider implies related-but-distinct groups; unrelated content belongs on separate pages or panels. Best Practices Use a labeled Divider (with text) only when the label adds real information ("Or"), not as decoration. Keep its weight and color subtle - a Divider should recede, not compete with the content it separates. Do and Don't Do Personal detailsBilling details Marks a real boundary between two distinct groups of fields, so the eye knows where one section ends. Don't First nameLast nameEmail A divider between every single field turns a short form into a fence of lines, drowning out the one grouping boundary that would actually help. Accessibility Purely decorative in most cases, so it's hidden from assistive technology rather than announced as content. When it also carries a semantic heading-like label, that label is exposed as real text, not baked into a background image. Never used as the sole way to convey a structural boundary that should really be a heading or landmark. pages.guide: Component Guide Human View Machine View Overview Drawer is a panel that slides in from a screen edge above a dimmed backdrop, for tasks that need more room than a Modal but shouldn't fully interrupt the page layout behind it - the page stays visible and contextually present at the edge, unlike Modal's fully centered takeover. When to Use An edit-in-place panel - editing a record's details without leaving the list behind it. A filter or settings side panel - adjusting options while keeping the underlying content in view. A detail preview or a multi-step form that needs more room than a dialog - still tied to the specific context it opened from. When Not to Use A short, focused decision or confirmation - use Modal - Drawer's larger size is unnecessary weight for a quick yes/no. Content meant to persist as part of the page's normal layout - use a permanent panel or sidebar rather than a Drawer that must be explicitly opened and closed. A brief, non-blocking status update - use Toast or Notification instead of a full sliding panel. Best Practices Keep the underlying page visible and dimmed, not hidden, so context isn't lost while the Drawer is open. Choose a consistent edge (commonly the right) for a given type of task across the product. Warn before closing a Drawer with unsaved changes, the same way you would for a Modal. Do and Don't Do FiltersStatus, owner and date range - applied to the list still visible behind. A side task with enough substance to fill the panel, kept beside the list it acts on rather than covering it. Don't Discard draft?CancelDiscard A one-line confirmation leaves most of the panel empty and still blocks the page to slide in. Use Modal or Pop Confirm when there is only a question to ask. Accessibility Traps keyboard focus within the panel while open, and restores it to the triggering element on close, matching Modal's behavior. Exposed as role="dialog" with aria-modal="true" and an accessible name (its title via aria-labelledby), announced as it opens - like Modal, this is focus management and an interrupting dialog, not a passive aria-live announcement. Escape and a visible close control are both always available, regardless of what task is in progress inside it. pages.guide: Component Guide Human View Machine View Overview Dropdown is a trigger button that reveals a list of actions or commands when clicked, like "More actions" or "Sort by" - distinct from Select, which picks a form value, and from the Menu panel it opens, which is a separate component in its own right. When to Use A row-level actions menu - opening a list of commands for a single table row. A bulk-actions or sort-by trigger - acting on multiple selected items, or choosing a sort order from a command list. A catch-all "more options" trigger - when several secondary actions don't fit as individual buttons. When Not to Use Picking a value that gets stored or submitted as form data - use Select - Dropdown triggers actions, it doesn't hold a form value. A single, common action that deserves its own visible button - don't bury a frequently-used action inside a Dropdown just to reduce button count. Persistent, always-visible navigation - use a nav bar, sidebar, or Tabs instead of hiding primary navigation behind a click. Best Practices Order menu items by frequency of use or logical grouping, with destructive actions visually separated at the bottom. Keep the trigger's label descriptive ("Sort by", not just an icon) unless the icon convention is already well established. Close the menu on selection, on outside click, and on Escape - never leave it open after an action fires. Do and Don't Do Sort by: Newest▾ The trigger states the current selection, so the control still reads correctly closed, without needing to be opened first. Don't Options▾ A generic "Options" label never reflects what has actually been chosen, so the user has to reopen the menu just to check the current state. Accessibility The trigger exposes aria-haspopup and aria-expanded, reflecting whether the menu is currently open. The opened menu is fully keyboard-navigable (arrow keys, Enter to activate, Escape to close) without requiring a mouse. Focus returns to the trigger when the menu closes, so keyboard users don't lose their place. pages.guide: Component Guide Human View Machine View Overview Empty stands in whenever a list, table, or search result has no data to show, so the space reads as intentionally empty rather than broken - an icon, a title, an optional description, and an optional action to resolve the empty state. When to Use A search with no matching results - explaining that nothing matched, not leaving a blank area. A brand-new or unused feature area - before the user has created their first item. An empty inbox, notification list, or shopping cart - any collection with genuinely zero items. When Not to Use Content that's still loading - use Skeleton or Spin - Empty means "confirmed nothing here," not "still checking." An error that prevented data from loading at all - use Result or an explicit error message - a failed fetch isn't the same as a legitimately empty result. A brief, non-blocking status update - use Toast or Alert instead of a full empty-state panel for something transient. Best Practices Explain why the space is empty and, when possible, what the user can do about it (e.g. "No results - try a different search"). Offer a direct action to resolve the state when one exists ("Create your first project"), not just a passive message. Keep the tone matter-of-fact rather than apologetic - an empty state is often a normal, expected condition, not a failure. Do and Don't Do No invoices yetInvoices you send will show up here.Create invoice Explains why the space is blank and offers the one action that would fill it, rather than leaving a dead end. Don't No data "No data" does not say whether that is because nothing has happened yet, a filter is hiding everything, or something failed - three states that each need a different message. Accessibility The message is real text, not baked into an illustration, so screen readers can announce it. Any resolving action is a real, keyboard-operable control, not just a static graphic. Decorative illustrations are marked so assistive technology doesn't announce them as meaningful content. pages.guide: Component Guide Human View Machine View Overview Float Button is a persistent, icon-only action anchored to a fixed corner of the screen, used for a single always-accessible action a user might need regardless of scroll position or context - distinct from an inline Button, which lives within the page's normal content flow. When to Use A persistent utility action - Back to top, Compose new item. A support or help launcher - a customer support chat entry point. A single primary page action that should stay reachable while scrolling - Quick add. When Not to Use Multiple competing floating actions on one screen - pick the single truly persistent action; route the rest through a menu or inline buttons. An action that already exists inline on the page - don't duplicate it as a float - that just adds visual noise. Complex, multi-step actions - a Float Button should trigger something simple or open another surface (Modal, Drawer) - it shouldn't carry the whole flow itself. Best Practices Use exactly one Float Button per screen so it stays meaningfully "the" persistent action. Choose an icon that is universally recognizable without a label (a plus, an upward arrow, a chat bubble). Reserve the badge dot for a real unread/pending count, not decoration. Always pair it with a tooltip, since the control itself carries no visible text. Do and Don't Do + Exactly one floating action, so it reliably means "the persistent thing you can always do here". Don't +✉⚙ A stack of floating buttons covers the content it floats over and turns a clear affordance into a second navigation bar. Accessibility Icon-only, so it needs an explicit aria-label naming the action - there is no visible text to fall back on. The tooltip is a supplementary visual hint, not a substitute for the accessible name. Keeps a full-size touch target even though it's visually compact, meeting WCAG 2.2 target-size guidance. pages.guide: Component Guide Human View Machine View Overview Group Button is a segmented control for switching between a small, fixed set of mutually exclusive options - one bordered strip of adjoining buttons where exactly one segment is active at a time, unlike Radio's separate circular inputs or Select's collapsed dropdown. When to Use A view toggle - switching between List and Grid layouts. A time range or sort filter - Day/Week/Month, or a sort-order picker. A short, fixed set of exclusive settings - unit system (Metric/Imperial), text alignment. When Not to Use More than five or six options - segments get cramped; use Select or Dropdown instead. Options that aren't mutually exclusive - use a Checkbox group so more than one can be active. A single on/off setting - use Switch - Group Button is for choosing among several options, not toggling one. Best Practices Keep segment labels short (a word or an icon) so they never wrap or truncate. Use it for exactly one active option at a time - it is not a multi-select control. Keep the segment count small enough to fit without horizontal scrolling on narrow screens. Do and Don't Do DayWeekMonth A short, fixed set of mutually exclusive options, each label a single word, all visible at once. Don't Last 24 hoursPrevious calendar week Sentence-length labels stretch the segments until the control no longer scans as a single row of choices. Use Select once labels get this long. Accessibility Exposed as a group of real buttons with aria-pressed reflecting each segment's active state. Visible focus ring per segment, independent of the active-state background fill. The active segment is communicated by more than color alone (a filled background, not just a text-color change). pages.guide: Component Guide Human View Machine View Overview Image displays a photo or graphic with graceful loading, error, and hover-preview states built in - a styled wrapper around a real image with defined placeholder, broken-image, and zoom-preview behavior, instead of a bare, unstyled tag with no fallback handling. When to Use A product gallery or article cover photo - any primary visual content that benefits from a defined loading/error state. User-generated content previews - images uploaded by users, which may occasionally fail to load. Document thumbnails or an avatar upload preview - anywhere an image needs consistent framing and fallback handling. When Not to Use A small identity graphic representing a person - use Avatar, which is purpose-built for that role, including initials fallback. A purely decorative background graphic with no meaningful content - a plain CSS background may be simpler than the full Image component's loading/error machinery. An icon - use the system's icon set rather than the Image component for small vector glyphs. Best Practices Always define a visible loading placeholder that matches the image's eventual aspect ratio, so the layout doesn't jump once it loads. Show a clear, distinct broken-image state (not just a blank box) when a URL fails to resolve. Use the hover-zoom/preview behavior only where inspecting detail actually matters (a product photo), not on every image site-wide. Do and Don't Do Warehouse floor plan, Level 2 A caption that says what the image actually is, useful the moment the picture itself fails to load. Don't Image No caption and no alt text means a failed image leaves nothing behind but an empty box - the content is simply gone for that user. Accessibility Every image carries meaningful alt text describing its content, or an empty alt when it's purely decorative. The broken-image fallback state is still announced meaningfully, not left as an unlabeled empty box. Zoom/preview interactions are reachable and dismissible by keyboard, not mouse-hover-only. pages.guide: Component Guide Human View Machine View Overview Input (Text Field) is the base single-line text control for collecting free-form values - a label, a text box with a placeholder, and states for focus, filled, error and disabled - the foundation every more specialized text field (Password, Number, Search, and others) builds on. When to Use Any short, free-form line of text - email address, full name, company name. A value with no fixed format the system can validate character-by-character - a search term typed into a form. A phone number or similar short structured value with no dedicated component - when no more specific field type exists. When Not to Use A value from a fixed, known list - use Select so the user picks rather than types a value that must match exactly. Multiple lines of text - use Text Area. A secret value that should stay hidden while typing - use Password. A value with a live suggestion list - use Autocomplete or Mention. Best Practices Always pair the field with a visible label, not placeholder-only text - placeholders disappear once typing starts and fail low-vision and memory-impaired users. Show validation errors inline, next to the field, with a specific message rather than a generic "Invalid input." Use placeholder text only for a format example (e.g. "name@company.com"), never as the only instruction for what to enter. Do and Don't Do Email address A visible label that stays put, with the placeholder showing the expected format rather than carrying the meaning. Don't A placeholder used as the label disappears the moment someone types, leaving the filled field unlabelled for anyone who looks away and back. Accessibility The label is programmatically associated with the input (via for/id or by wrapping it), not just visually adjacent. The error state sets aria-invalid and links the error message with aria-describedby, so screen readers announce it. Focus state shows a visible outline distinct from the field's default border. pages.guide: Component Guide Human View Machine View Overview Mention is a free-form text field that lets someone tag another person inline by typing "@" followed by a name, inserting a distinct chip in the middle of otherwise normal text - used for comments, chat, and any message field where notifying a specific person matters. Code review and support ticket threads - notifying a specific reviewer or agent. When Not to Use A field whose sole purpose is picking one person from a list - use Select or Autocomplete instead of a full free-text field with an embedded picker. Plain free-form text with no need to tag anyone - use Input or Text Area - the "@" trigger adds complexity that's wasted if never used. Tagging concepts, labels, or categories rather than people - use Tag or a multi-select Select instead of overloading the mention pattern. Best Practices Trigger the suggestion panel immediately on "@" and filter it live as the user keeps typing a name. Let the user keep typing free-form text before and after a mention - it should never take over the whole field. pages.guide: Component Guide Human View Machine View Overview Menu is the floating panel of commands or actions itself - what appears when a Dropdown trigger, a right-click, or a "..." button is activated. This component is the panel/list content, not the trigger that opens it, which is a separate concern handled by Dropdown or a custom trigger. A user account menu or bulk-actions panel - any floating list of clickable commands triggered from elsewhere. When Not to Use The trigger button itself - that's Dropdown's responsibility - Menu is only the panel content. A form value picker - use Select - Menu items are commands to run, not values to store. Persistent, always-visible navigation - use a nav bar or sidebar rather than a menu that must be triggered open. Best Practices Group related items with dividers, and visually separate destructive actions (e.g. "Delete") at the bottom. Keep item labels as short, specific verbs ("Duplicate", "Archive") so the whole menu scans quickly. Close on selection, outside click, and Escape, consistent with Dropdown's expected behavior. Do and Don't Do RenameDuplicateDelete A top border separates the destructive action from the routine ones, so it cannot be clicked by momentum. Don't DeleteRenameDuplicate Placing Delete first, right where the pointer lands on open, makes the riskiest action the easiest one to trigger by accident. Accessibility Implemented with menu/menuitem roles, so arrow keys move between items and Home/End jump to the first/last item. pages.guide: Component Guide Human View Machine View Overview Modal is a dialog box that appears above a dimmed backdrop to focus the user on one task or decision before returning them to the page - it blocks interaction with everything behind it until the user responds or explicitly closes it. When to Use A destructive-action confirmation - confirming a delete before it happens. A short, focused task or form - terms acceptance, an onboarding step. A media preview that needs full attention - viewing an image or document in detail. When Not to Use A task that needs more room than a dialog comfortably allows - use Drawer, which slides in from an edge instead of interrupting the whole page. A brief, non-blocking confirmation - use Toast or Alert - Modal's backdrop is a heavy interruption for something minor. Frequent or repeated interruptions in a single flow - excessive modal use breaks flow; consider inline validation or a Drawer instead. Best Practices Give it a single clear purpose and a single primary action - avoid turning it into a small multi-purpose page. Always provide an obvious way to close it (a visible close button and Escape), even when a primary action is required. Keep destructive confirmations short and specific about the consequence, not a generic "Are you sure?" Do and Don't Do Delete 3 files?This cannot be undone.CancelDelete One decision, stated with its consequence, and a button that names the action rather than agreeing vaguely. Don't Are you sure?Please confirm.NoYes "Are you sure?" with Yes/No never says what is about to happen, so the user confirms without knowing what they agreed to. pages.guide: Component Guide Human View Machine View Overview Notification is a corner-anchored card that reports a background or async event - an icon, bold title, longer description, and a close button, with an optional action - used for events the user wasn't necessarily watching for, unlike Toast's brief confirmation of an action just taken. When to Use A background task completing - an async upload or export finishing while the user was doing something else. A new message or mention alert - an event unrelated to what's currently on screen. A system status change or a stack of several notifications - more content or more persistence than Toast is built for. When Not to Use A quick confirmation of an action the user just took - use Toast - it's lighter and self-dismisses faster. A message embedded in the page's own content flow - use Alert. A decision the user must make before continuing - use Modal or Pop Confirm - Notification is informational, not a blocking choice. Best Practices Give it a real title and description, not just a one-line message - that extra structure is what distinguishes it from Toast. Stack multiple notifications clearly rather than replacing one before it's been read. Only include an action button when there's a genuinely useful next step (e.g. "View"), not by default. Do and Don't Do Export finishedreport-q1.csv is ready to download. Reports a background job the user was not watching, with enough detail to act on later. Don't Saved A one-word confirmation of something the user just did belongs in a Toast. Notification's weight is meant for events they did not initiate. Accessibility Announced via an aria-live region so it reaches screen-reader users even if their focus is elsewhere on the page. The close control is independently focusable and labeled ("Dismiss notification"). Persists long enough (or until manually dismissed) to be read in full, unlike Toast's short auto-dismiss window. pages.guide: Component Guide Human View Machine View Overview Number is a text field restricted to numeric input, optionally paired with stepper buttons to increment or decrement the value by a fixed amount - used anywhere the value is fundamentally a quantity rather than arbitrary text. When to Use A quantity someone adjusts up or down - cart quantity, guest count. Any purely numeric value - age, price, a rating count. A bounded value with a sensible min/max and step - where steppers make small adjustments faster than typing. When Not to Use A number that's really an identifier, not a quantity - a phone number, a ZIP/postal code, a credit card number - use Input, since these are never incremented/decremented and often contain formatting characters. A value that should be picked from a fixed list - use Select. A range of two numbers - consider Slider for a bounded range with no need for exact keyboard entry. Best Practices Set sensible min/max/step values that match the real-world constraint (e.g. quantity can't go below 1). Keep the stepper buttons a secondary input method - typing a value directly should always work too. Show units alongside the field (e.g. "kg", "$") rather than expecting the number alone to communicate meaning. Do and Don't Do Quantity+-1 to 20 per order. Steppers for a small count the user nudges, with the permitted range stated up front. Don't Salary+- Steppers on a value in the tens of thousands are useless - nobody clicks up from zero. Drop them when the step is not a unit the user thinks in. Accessibility Uses the native numeric input semantics so mobile keyboards default to a numeric layout automatically. Stepper buttons are separately focusable and labeled ("Increase quantity" / "Decrease quantity"), not just plus/minus icons. pages.guide: Component Guide Human View Machine View Overview Pagination lets someone navigate through pages of a large result set, like search results or a data table - numbered page controls (or a simple Prev/Next pair) plus a page count, so a huge dataset stays browsable without loading everything at once. When to Use Search results split across pages - a results list too long to show all at once. A data table with many rows - an admin grid or report view. A product listing or blog archive - any large, ordered collection browsed a page at a time. When Not to Use A small result set that fits on one screen - pagination adds unnecessary interaction for a handful of items. A feed the user scrolls continuously through - use infinite scroll or a "load more" pattern instead of discrete pages, if that better matches the content type. Navigating between unrelated sections of a product - use Tabs, a nav bar, or Breadcrumb - Pagination is only for moving within one ordered result set. Best Practices Always show which page is currently active and, when feasible, the total number of pages or results. Provide direct jump controls (first/last, or a page-number input) for very large result sets, not just Prev/Next. Keep the control's position consistent (commonly below the content it paginates) across every paginated view. pages.guide: Component Guide Human View Machine View Overview Password is a text field that masks its characters by default, with a toggle to reveal the value temporarily - used for any secret the user is actively typing, so it stays hidden from anyone glancing at the screen while still letting the user verify what they typed. When to Use Login and sign-up forms - collecting an account password. A PIN code or short secret - still worth masking even if numeric. Changing a password or entering an API key - any value that shouldn't be visible by default. When Not to Use A value that isn't actually secret - use Input - masking non-sensitive data only adds friction. A one-time code delivered separately and meant to be read back to someone - consider whether masking helps or just adds a step; a plain Input or Number field may serve better. Multi-line secret content - Password is single-line only; there's no dedicated masked textarea in this system. Best Practices Always provide the show/hide toggle - masking with no way to verify what was typed increases error rates and failed submissions. Never restrict paste into a password field; blocking paste actively discourages the use of password managers. Show password strength or requirement feedback near the field, not only after a failed submit. Do and Don't Do PasswordAt least 12 characters. States the rule before the user types, and lets them reveal what they entered so a typo is fixable rather than guessable. Don't PasswordPassword does not meet requirements. Hiding the rule until after submission, with no way to see what was typed, makes the user retry blind against a standard they still have not been told. Accessibility The show/hide toggle has an accessible name that reflects its current state ("Show password" / "Hide password"), not just an icon. Toggling visibility keeps keyboard focus on the field, so the user isn't forced to re-locate it. The input still exposes autocomplete hints (current-password / new-password) so password managers can assist correctly. pages.guide: Component Guide Human View Machine View Overview Pop Confirm asks a short "are you sure?" question right next to the trigger that caused it, with Confirm/Cancel buttons inline in the popover - a lightweight alternative to a full Modal for confirmations that don't need to fully block the page. When to Use A delete or remove confirmation on a single row or item - anchored right at the action that triggered it. Discarding unsaved changes or leaving a page - a quick check before a potentially costly action. A bulk action or an irreversible toggle confirmation - still simple enough not to need a full dialog. When Not to Use A decision with real complexity or multiple fields - use Modal - Pop Confirm is for a single yes/no question, not a form. An action with severe, hard-to-reverse consequences at scale - consider a full Modal with more explicit warning copy for genuinely high-stakes confirmations. Something that isn't actually a confirmation - use Popover for general contextual content that isn't a yes/no decision. Best Practices Keep the question and both button labels short and specific ("Delete this file?" / "Delete" / "Cancel"). Anchor it directly to the triggering control so the connection between action and confirmation is obvious. Close it on an outside click or Escape without treating that as a confirmation either way. Do and Don't Do Delete this file?CancelDelete A single yes-or-no question, anchored to the control that triggered it, with buttons that name the outcome. Don't Delete this file? Also remove it from shared folders, revoke links, and notify collaborators?NoOK Several decisions bundled into one question cannot be answered with one button. Once it needs this much explaining, use a Modal. Accessibility Pop Confirm exists to gate a destructive or otherwise irreversible action, so its popover content carries role="alertdialog" rather than a plain popover/tooltip role - that's what gets its appearance and question announced together as a single interruption, instead of relying on the user to notice it visually. Focus moves into the alertdialog (typically onto the Cancel button, the safer default) when it opens, and returns to the exact triggering element when it closes, whether closed by Confirm, Cancel, Escape, or an outside click. The Confirm and Cancel buttons are distinguishable by more than color, especially when Confirm is destructive-styled. Escape closes it exactly like a Cancel, never like a silent Confirm. pages.guide: Component Guide Human View Machine View Overview Popover shows contextual details, a quick action, or a small settings panel next to a trigger element, opened by a click rather than a hover - richer and more persistent than Tooltip, since it stays open until the user dismisses it or clicks elsewhere. When to Use Contextual details revealed on click - more information than a hover-only Tooltip can comfortably hold. An inline help panel or a quick-actions menu - a small floating panel anchored to its trigger. A filter/settings mini-panel or a user-info preview - richer content that benefits from staying open while the user reads or interacts with it. When Not to Use A short, single-line hint - use Tooltip - Popover is heavier than a brief label needs. A yes/no confirmation with Confirm/Cancel actions - use Pop Confirm, which is purpose-built for that exact pattern. Content that should fully block the rest of the page - use Modal or Drawer instead of a lightweight anchored panel. Best Practices Keep the content focused and scoped to what the trigger is about - a Popover shouldn't turn into a secondary page. Close it on outside click and Escape, consistent with other floating-panel components. Anchor it reliably to its trigger even as the page scrolls or resizes, so it never floats disconnected from context. Do and Don't Do Storage almost full92% used. Free up space or upgrade your plan.ⓘ A short title plus one or two lines of real detail - richer than a Tooltip, but still small enough to read at a glance. Don't Account settingsFull profile editing, notification preferences, connected apps, billing history and two-factor setup all live here - update anything and it saves immediately across every device you are signed into.ⓘ A popover this dense is really a page pretending to float. Once it needs paragraphs, send the user to a real settings screen instead. Accessibility The trigger exposes aria-expanded and aria-haspopup, reflecting the popover's open state. Focus moves into the popover when it opens and returns to the trigger when it closes. Interactive content inside it (buttons, links) remains fully keyboard-reachable in a sensible tab order. pages.guide: Component Guide Human View Machine View Overview Progress shows how far a quantifiable operation has gotten toward completion, like an upload or a multi-step setup flow, rendered as either a linear bar or a circular ring - used whenever a real percentage or fraction is known, unlike Spin which has no known completion point. When to Use A file upload or download - a measurable percentage complete. Multi-step onboarding completion or storage/quota usage - a proportion of a known total. Skill/profile completeness or a long-running task with a known percentage - anywhere "how much is done" is the useful information. When Not to Use An operation with no known duration or percentage - use Spin instead - Progress implies a measurable fraction, and showing a fake one is misleading. A step-based flow better represented by discrete stages than a continuous percentage - use Steps. A single instantaneous action with no meaningful "in progress" period - Progress adds nothing for actions that resolve immediately. Best Practices Only show a percentage or fill amount that reflects real, measured progress - never a fake or purely cosmetic animation. Pair the bar/ring with a visible percentage or fraction label when precision matters to the user. Use the circular ring for compact spaces and the linear bar when there's room for a full-width indicator. Do and Don't Do 65% One bar for the whole operation, carrying a real measured fraction, so the user can answer "how much longer" at a glance. Don't 100%40%0% A bar per sub-step makes the user add up the pieces to work out where the operation actually is. Report one number for the whole job. Accessibility Exposed with role="progressbar", including aria-valuenow, aria-valuemin, and aria-valuemax - visible in the Do/Don't demo markup above - so assistive technology can read the current, minimum and maximum values on demand. No separate aria-live region is layered on top of role="progressbar": the widget's value attributes already let a screen reader announce progress when the user chooses to check it, and a role="progressbar" element is exposed with an implicit live-region-like behavior in most screen readers, so adding an explicit aria-live would just risk duplicate or overly chatty announcements as the value updates. Color is never the only way completion or error state is communicated. Updates are announced at reasonable intervals, not so frequently that they become noisy for screen-reader users. pages.guide: Component Guide Human View Machine View Overview Rating is a row of identical icon buttons (stars or hearts) that fill in as the user hovers or taps, letting someone score something on a simple, bounded scale - built for quick, low-friction feedback rather than precise numeric entry. When to Use A product or service review score - a 0-5 star rating. A quick satisfaction survey question - how satisfied were you, on a small fixed scale. A content quality score - used internally to flag good or poor examples. When Not to Use A precise numeric value - use Number - Rating is for a small, discrete, low-precision scale, not exact figures. A scale bigger than a handful of points - beyond roughly 5-10 points, individual icons stop being scannable at a glance; consider Slider or Number instead. A binary yes/no signal - use Switch or a simple Checkbox rather than a rating scale for a single up/down choice. Best Practices Preview the would-be selection on hover before it's committed by a click/tap, so users can see what they're about to choose. Keep the icon count small and fixed (commonly 5) - a rating scale should be scannable in a single glance. Pair the icon row with a numeric or text label when precision matters (e.g. "4.5 out of 5"), since icons alone can't show fractional values clearly. Do and Don't Do Rate this article A single five-point scale for one clear question - quick to answer and quick to read back in aggregate. Don't AccuracyToneDepthUsefulness Four scales turn a two-second reaction into a survey, and most people abandon it rather than score every dimension. Accessibility Each icon is an independently focusable, labeled control ("Rate 3 out of 5"), not one giant unlabeled row. pages.guide: Component Guide Human View Machine View Overview Result is a full-panel outcome screen that reports a multi-step flow completing or failing - a large semantic icon, bold title, description, and one or two action buttons occupying the main content area, so the user gets a clear, prominent outcome instead of an ambiguous blank or half-updated screen. When to Use Checkout or payment completion - a clear success screen after a purchase. The outcome of a multi-step form submission - success or failure as the flow's final screen. An error page (404/403) or a bulk operation summary - any full-page outcome, positive or negative. When Not to Use A minor, in-flow confirmation that doesn't warrant a dedicated full-page screen - use Toast, Alert, or Notification instead. An intermediate step where the user still has more to do - use Steps or Progress to show partial completion, not Result, which implies an ending. A quick inline validation message - Result is for the end of a flow, not error feedback on individual fields. Best Practices Make the primary next action unmistakable ("Go to dashboard", "Try again") rather than leaving the user without a clear path forward. Match the icon and tone precisely to the outcome - a success icon on a failed operation is actively confusing. Keep the description specific about what happened and, for failures, what the user can do next. Do and Don't Do Payment failedYour card was declined. Try another card.Try again Ends the flow with a clear outcome and one obvious way forward. Don't Payment failedError code 402. An outcome screen with no next step strands the user at a dead end holding a code that means nothing to them. Accessibility No aria-live region is added here on purpose. Result is a static post-action page occupying the main content area - like an order-confirmation screen - not a status dynamically injected into an otherwise-unchanged page the user might not be looking at. It is reached the same way any new page/view is: by a route change or full content swap, so the ordinary mechanism for that (moving focus to the page, e.g. its heading, and/or updating the document title) already tells screen-reader users the flow has ended. Wrapping it in aria-live would be redundant with, and can even fight, that page-level announcement. Because of that, the outcome (success/failure) is communicated in text, not by icon or color alone. As the primary content of the page, its heading receives focus (or is otherwise announced via the page's normal load/route-change handling) so screen-reader users immediately know the flow has ended, without relying on a live region to do that job. Action buttons use specific, descriptive labels, not generic "OK" or "Continue" with no context. pages.guide: Component Guide Human View Machine View Overview Search is a text field purpose-built for querying or filtering a set of content - it intentionally skips a visible label by convention, since a search icon and placeholder text make its purpose obvious in the contexts it's used. When to Use Global or site-wide search - a top-level search bar. Filtering a table, list, or dataset already on screen - narrowing visible rows as the user types. A command palette or inbox search - any live-filtering query field. When Not to Use A value submitted as part of a larger form - use Input - Search implies live querying, not form submission. A field that needs a visible, persistent label for clarity (e.g. in a dense settings form) - use Input with a label instead of relying on the search icon alone. A field that should suggest specific matching values as you type - use Autocomplete if suggestions, not just filtering, are the goal. Best Practices Debounce the query as the user types rather than searching on every keystroke, especially for server-side search. Always include a visible clear ('x') control once text has been entered. Show a clear empty-results state when a query returns nothing, rather than leaving a blank list. Do and Don't Do ×Searches file names and contents. Says what is being searched, and offers a clear affordance so the user can get back to the unfiltered list in one action. Don't With no scope stated and no way to clear, an empty result set is unreadable - the user cannot tell whether nothing matched or they searched the wrong thing. Accessibility Even without a visible label, the field carries an accessible name (via aria-label or a visually hidden label) so screen readers announce its purpose. The clear button is independently focusable and labeled ("Clear search"), not just an icon with no accessible name. Live-updating results are announced via an aria-live region so screen-reader users know the list changed.
