pages.guide: Component Guide Human View Machine View Overview Select is a trigger field that opens a panel of predefined options, letting the user pick exactly one value from a known, fixed set - visually similar to Input but read-only and paired with a chevron, distinct from Dropdown (which triggers actions, not a form value) and Cascader (multi-level drill-down). When to Use A value from a known, fixed set - country, state/province, category. Sort order or similar single-choice configuration - Newest first, Price low to high. A language or locale picker - any small-to-medium closed option list. When Not to Use Free-form text with no fixed set of valid values - use Input. Hierarchical or nested data - use Cascader (linked columns) or Tree Select (an expandable tree). Selecting more than one value at a time - use a multi-select variant, Checkbox group, or Transfer. A very large option list better filtered by typing - use Autocomplete instead of scrolling a long panel. Best Practices Order options logically - alphabetical, by frequency of use, or with a sensible default first. Show an explicit placeholder like "Select an option" rather than silently pre-selecting an arbitrary value. Truncate long option labels gracefully in the closed trigger rather than letting them overflow the field. Do and Don't Do CountrySelect a country An explicit placeholder makes it obvious nothing has been chosen yet, so an untouched field cannot be mistaken for a decision. Don't CountryAfghanistan Pre-selecting the alphabetically-first option silently submits an answer nobody gave. pages.guide: Component Guide Human View Machine View Overview Skeleton stands in for content that hasn't finished loading yet - stacked text lines, an avatar with text, or a card-shaped placeholder - so the layout doesn't jump once real content arrives, and the wait feels shorter than a blank screen or a generic spinner. When to Use Initial page or data load - showing the eventual layout's shape before content arrives. Infinite scroll or async feed content - placeholders for rows or cards not yet loaded. Profile/avatar loading or dashboard widgets - any content whose eventual shape is known in advance. When Not to Use A loading state with no predictable content shape - use Spin - Skeleton relies on knowing roughly what will appear. A brief, sub-second load - a flash of skeleton UI can feel more distracting than a near-instant content swap; reserve it for loads long enough to actually help. An operation with a known percentage of completion - use Progress, which communicates real completion, not just "still loading." Best Practices Match the skeleton's shape closely to the real content's eventual layout, so the transition feels seamless rather than jarring. Use a subtle shimmer or pulse animation to signal "still loading" rather than a static gray block that could be mistaken for an error. Swap it out the moment real content is ready - don't hold it past the actual load time. Do and Don't Do Placeholders shaped like the content that is coming, so nothing jumps when it arrives. Don't A single generic bar that looks nothing like the eventual layout gives no hint of what is loading, and the page still lurches when it lands. Accessibility The containing placeholder carries aria-busy="true" and aria-live="polite" (shown on the demo markup above), not just visual shimmer - silence during load reads as broken to a screen-reader user, who gets no equivalent of seeing shapes animate on screen. Once real content replaces it, the same live region's contents are swapped for the real DOM, so its arrival is announced too, and aria-busy is cleared to false. Purely decorative beyond that announcement - it never receives keyboard focus itself. pages.guide: Component Guide Human View Machine View Overview Slider lets someone pick a numeric value, or a range of two values, by dragging a thumb along a track - used for continuous or coarse-grained values where the exact number matters less than quickly finding the right position, like a volume level or a price filter. A single date or time value - use Date Picker or Time - a slider doesn't communicate calendar or clock context. pages.guide: Component Guide Human View Machine View Overview Spin indicates that something is happening with no known duration or completion percentage - a small ring that spins continuously until the operation finishes, used whenever there's genuinely no measurable progress to show. When to Use An inline button loading state - showing an action is in flight after a click. Section or panel content loading with no known shape or percentage - a generic in-progress signal. An async search, filter, or form submission in flight - any short wait with no meaningful progress fraction. When Not to Use An operation with a real, known percentage complete - use Progress instead - showing a spinner when real progress data exists hides useful information. Content whose eventual shape is already known - use Skeleton so the layout doesn't jump once it loads. A wait long enough that the user needs more context (time remaining, what's happening) - pair Spin with actual status text, or reconsider whether Progress fits better. Best Practices Keep it small and contextual - inline in a button or panel, not a full-page takeover unless the whole page truly depends on it. Pair it with a brief label ("Loading...", "Searching...") when the context alone doesn't make the wait obvious. Disable the control it's attached to while spinning, so the same action can't be triggered twice. Do and Don't Do Searching... Used where there is genuinely no percentage to report, and paired with a word about what is happening. Don't A bare spinner on a long wait leaves the user unable to tell progress from a hang. Add a label, or use Progress when the total is known. Accessibility Carries role="status" (or aria-live="polite" plus aria-busy="true") on the spinning element itself - a screen-reader user must hear that loading has started and hear again when it ends, since the ring's motion is entirely invisible to them. Never the only feedback for a long wait - pair with text for anything beyond a couple of seconds, and make sure that text is inside the same live region so its updates are announced too. pages.guide: Component Guide Human View Machine View Overview Splitter is a resizable two-panel layout with a draggable divider between them - the user drags the divider to redistribute space between the two panels, and either panel can optionally collapse to a thin strip to temporarily reclaim its space. When to Use A resizable sidebar next to a main content area - a file tree, a navigation panel, or a filters panel. A code editor and its live preview pane - both panels visible, resizable to taste. A master/detail layout - a list panel and a detail panel, like a chat list next to a conversation pane. When Not to Use A fixed layout where resizing adds no value - don't add a Splitter just because two things sit side by side; only when the user genuinely benefits from adjusting the ratio. Narrow or mobile viewports - a draggable divider is impractical on touch-first layouts; stack the panels instead. More than two panels needing independent resizing - nest multiple Splitters deliberately rather than trying to force one divider to manage three or more regions. Best Practices Persist the user's chosen split ratio across sessions when the layout is one they'll return to repeatedly. Enforce sensible minimum sizes on both panels so neither can be dragged down to an unusable sliver. Make the divider's hit target noticeably wider than its visible line, so it's easy to grab precisely. Do and Don't Do File treeEditor Two panels the user genuinely wants to resize against each other, with a visible drag handle marking the boundary. Don't IconsMain content A 15%-wide panel gives the user almost nothing to drag toward - there is no meaningful second layout to resize into. Use a fixed Sidebar instead. Accessibility The divider is a real, keyboard-operable control (arrow keys nudge the split ratio), not a mouse-only drag handle. The divider exposes its current position and valid range to assistive technology, similar to a slider. A collapsed panel's expand control has an accessible name identifying which panel it restores. pages.guide: Component Guide Human View Machine View Overview Statistic displays a single quantifiable number prominently - a title above a large, bold value, with an optional prefix (like a currency symbol), suffix (like a unit or percent sign), and a colored trend indicator - built for dashboard tiles and summary cards where one number needs to stand out at a glance. When to Use A dashboard KPI tile - active users, total revenue, open tickets. A metric with a trend - growth or decline versus a prior period, shown with a colored arrow. A live counter or a countdown - a value that updates over time but is always shown as one prominent number. When Not to Use Several related numbers that need to be compared side by side in rows and columns - use Table or Description instead of several standalone Statistic tiles. A number the user needs to edit - use Number or Input; Statistic is read-only, display-only. A value with no real numeric significance - a plain label or Tag communicates a status better than dressing it up as a number. Best Practices Keep the title short and unambiguous - a viewer should know exactly what the number represents without extra context. Format large numbers with separators (112,893, not 112893) so they're readable at a glance - use the locale-correct separator from Data Format rather than hard-coding a comma, since Statistic itself doesn't define number formatting. Reserve the positive/negative trend coloring for values that are genuinely good or bad news - don't color a neutral count green or red by default. Do and Don't Do Monthly active users48,204▲ 12% One number, labelled plainly, with the trend that gives it meaning - up from what, and by how much. Don't Users48,204.37 Raw unrounded precision on a headline number reads as noise, not confidence - it forces the reader to mentally truncate it themselves. Accessibility The title and value are both real text, read together by screen readers as one meaningful statement, not conveyed by size or color alone. Trend direction is stated in text or via an icon with an accessible label ("up 12.5%"), not communicated by arrow shape or color alone. The loading state is marked so assistive technology announces that the value is not yet available, rather than reading an empty placeholder. pages.guide: Component Guide Human View Machine View Overview Steps shows position within a multi-step flow, like a checkout or onboarding wizard - numbered circles connected by a line, each marked completed, current, or upcoming, so the user always knows how far along they are and what's left. pages.guide: Component Guide Human View Machine View Overview Switch is for instantly toggling a single, independent setting on or off - the change takes effect immediately with no separate confirm or submit step, unlike a Checkbox inside a form that waits for the whole form to be submitted. When to Use A setting that applies the moment it's flipped - a notification toggle, dark mode. A feature flag or experimental setting - turned on/off independently of any form. A device-level or system-level toggle - airplane mode. When Not to Use A setting that needs explicit confirmation before it takes effect - use Checkbox plus a Save button, or a confirmation dialog for risky changes. More than two states - Switch is strictly binary; use Group Button or Select for three or more options. A choice that's part of a larger form submitted together - Checkbox communicates that context more clearly than an instantly-applied Switch. Best Practices Label the setting by its "on" state clearly ("Notifications", not "Enable") so the label reads correctly in both positions. Reflect the change immediately in whatever the switch controls, so the user gets instant confirming feedback. Avoid using Switch for anything destructive or hard to reverse without pairing it with a follow-up confirmation. Do and Don't Do Dark mode Named for the setting itself, and it applies the instant it is flipped - no Save step to hunt for. Don't Enable dark mode setting?Save A Switch that only takes effect after a separate Save contradicts what a switch promises. Use a Checkbox when the change is submitted with a form. Accessibility Exposed with a real switch or checkbox role, with the current state (on/off) announced to assistive technology. The label describes the setting itself, not the mechanism ("Dark mode", not "Toggle switch"). On/off is never communicated by color alone - the thumb's position and track fill both change too. pages.guide: Component Guide Human View Machine View Overview Table displays structured data across fixed columns, like an admin data grid or a report view - rows and columns that let a user compare values across many records at once, unlike List's simpler stacked-row layout with no column alignment. When to Use An admin data grid or user management list - structured records compared across shared columns. Order history or a report/analytics view - tabular data where column alignment aids comparison. An inventory listing - any dataset naturally organized into consistent fields per row. When Not to Use A simple stack of similar items with no meaningful column structure - use List instead - Table's column overhead isn't worth it for unstructured rows. A small number of visually distinct content blocks - use Card or a grid of Cards. Data better suited to a single set of label/value pairs - use Description for one record's details rather than a one-row table. Best Practices Keep column headers concise and consistently aligned with their column's data type (numbers right-aligned, text left-aligned). Support sorting on columns where order genuinely helps comparison, and clearly indicate the active sort. Pair large tables with pagination, virtualized scrolling, or both - virtualize once a table is showing 500+ rows, rather than rendering thousands of rows at once. pages.guide: Component Guide Human View Machine View Overview Tabs switch between a small, fixed set of related views or sections with exactly one active at a time - a horizontal row of triggers above the content they control, used when several views belong together but only one needs to be visible at once. When to Use Settings pages split into related sections - Profile, Security, Notifications. A product detail's content panes - Overview, Specifications, Reviews. Dashboard or account views sharing the same context - switching between related views without leaving the page. When Not to Use A sequence the user moves through in order, with a clear beginning and end - use Steps instead of Tabs, which implies free switching, not progression. More views than fit comfortably in a single row - beyond roughly 5-7 tabs, consider a Menu, Dropdown, or a redesigned navigation instead of a horizontally scrolling tab bar. Views that aren't actually related - unrelated destinations belong in real navigation (a sidebar, a Breadcrumb-backed hierarchy), not a tab set implying siblings. Best Practices Keep tab labels short and parallel in structure (all nouns, or all short phrases) so the row scans easily. Preserve the active tab across a page reload or back navigation when the URL or state allows it. Avoid nesting tabs within tabs - it quickly becomes disorienting to track which level is active. Do and Don't Do DetailsActivitySettings A handful of parallel views over the same object, one visibly active, each reachable in a single click. Don't OverviewDetailsActivityCommentsHistoryPermissionsBillingIntegrations Eight tabs forces the row to scroll sideways, so most of them are invisible until the user thinks to swipe. Group the overflow into a Menu or a nested page instead. Accessibility Implemented with tab/tabpanel roles, so arrow keys move between tabs and the association between a tab and its panel is explicit. The active tab is exposed via aria-selected, not communicated by color alone. pages.guide: Component Guide Human View Machine View Overview Time is a text field with a fixed trailing clock icon that opens a time picker for selecting a time of day - the temporal counterpart to Date Picker, used whenever the value is a time rather than a calendar date. When to Use A meeting or event start time - any specific time of day. A reminder or alarm - a time with no associated calendar date. Store hours or an appointment slot - a time chosen from within a day. When Not to Use A calendar date - use Date Picker. Both a date and a time together - pair Date Picker and Time as two fields, or use a combined date-time pattern if the product defines one - Time alone doesn't carry a date. A duration rather than a point in time - e.g. "2 hours" - use Number with a unit label instead. Best Practices Respect the user's locale for 12-hour vs. 24-hour display, rather than hard-coding one format. Snap the picker to a sensible interval (e.g. 15 minutes) when exact-to-the-second precision isn't meaningful. Let the user type a time directly as an alternative to scrolling/clicking through the picker. Do and Don't Do Meeting starts09:30Your local time (GMT+1). Names the timezone the number is in, which is the only thing that makes a time shared between people actionable. Don't Meeting starts09:30 A bare time is ambiguous the moment two people in different places read it, and neither of them will notice until one misses the meeting. Accessibility The time picker is fully keyboard-operable (arrow keys or typing to adjust hour/minute, Enter to confirm). The field's accessible name states what the time represents ("Meeting start time"), not just "Time". AM/PM (in 12-hour format) is exposed as its own clearly labeled control, not bundled invisibly into the hour value. pages.guide: Component Guide Human View Machine View Overview Timeline shows a sequence of events in chronological order, each with a dot connected by a continuous line - used for activity logs, order status history, or a project's milestone history, so the reader can see what happened, when, and in what order. When to Use Order status history - showing each stage a shipment or order has passed through. An activity or audit log - chronological events tied to a record. Project milestone tracking or onboarding progress - a sequence of events, each with a point in time. When Not to Use A fixed sequence the user is actively moving through right now - use Steps instead - Timeline is a historical record, Steps is an in-progress flow. Unordered or non-chronological content - a Timeline's core value is chronological order; don't use it for a list with no meaningful sequence. A simple list with no time dimension at all - use List. Best Practices Keep each entry's timestamp visible and consistently formatted, since chronology is the whole point of a Timeline. Use distinct icons or colors sparingly, reserved for genuinely different event types, not decoration. For very long histories, consider collapsing older entries or paginating rather than rendering the entire history at once. Do and Don't Do Order shipped14 Mar, 09:12Out for deliveryExpected 16 Mar Events in chronological order, each with a timestamp, so the sequence and its pacing are both readable. Don't Out for deliveryOrder shipped Events out of order with no timestamps leave the reader unable to tell what actually happened when - the one thing a timeline exists to show. Accessibility Each entry's timestamp and description are real text, read in order by screen readers, not implied only by visual position on the line. The connecting line and dots are decorative and hidden from assistive technology - the meaningful content is the entry text itself. Event type (success, error, pending) is distinguishable by more than color, using an icon or text label as well. pages.guide: Component Guide Human View Machine View Overview Toast is a temporary, floating confirmation of an action or status change, typically surfaced in a fixed screen corner rather than embedded inline like Alert - it appears, communicates its message, and disappears on its own without requiring the user to stay put. When to Use A brief confirmation after an action - upload complete, copy-to-clipboard confirmation. An undo prompt - a short window to reverse the action just taken. A background job completing or a connection status change - events the user doesn't need to actively wait for. When Not to Use A message that needs to stay visible until manually dismissed or resolved - use Alert, which is embedded and persistent, not self-dismissing. Anything requiring a decision before the user can continue - use Modal or Pop Confirm - a self-dismissing Toast is the wrong place for a choice with consequences. Detailed or long-form content - use Notification, which is built for a longer title/description pairing. Best Practices Keep the message short enough to read in the few seconds before it disappears. Stack multiple toasts rather than replacing one before the user has had a chance to read it. Give an undo action a genuinely sufficient window before the toast dismisses, if undo is offered at all. Do and Don't Do Draft saved Short enough to read in the couple of seconds it is on screen, confirming something the user just did. Don't Delete this workspace?This removes all 240 files permanently. A decision inside a toast can vanish before it is answered. Anything with consequences belongs in a Modal or Pop Confirm. Accessibility Announced via an aria-live region so screen-reader users are told about it without needing to be focused on it. Long enough on-screen duration (or a pause-on-hover/focus behavior) so it doesn't disappear before it can be read or acted on. Any inline action (like Undo) is a real, independently focusable control. pages.guide: Component Guide Human View Machine View Overview Tooltip adds a short hint next to a trigger element, like an icon-only button, without needing to click anything - a small floating label that appears on hover or focus and disappears when attention moves elsewhere. When to Use Labeling an icon-only control - explaining what an unlabeled icon button does. Disclosing truncated text - showing the full value of text cut off with an ellipsis. A keyboard shortcut hint or a brief explanation for a disabled control - why an action currently can't be taken. When Not to Use Essential information the user must see to complete a task - hover-only content is easy to miss, especially on touch devices; put critical information visibly on screen instead. Long or multi-paragraph content - use Popover, which supports richer content and stays open until dismissed. Content that needs to remain visible while the user interacts with it - a tooltip disappears when hover/focus moves away, so it can't hold interactive controls of its own. Best Practices Keep the text to a single short phrase or sentence - if it needs more, use Popover instead. Trigger it on both hover and keyboard focus, never hover alone, so keyboard users get the same information. Avoid delaying its appearance so long that it feels unresponsive, or so little that it flickers on incidental mouse movement. Do and Don't Do Archive□ Supplies the name of an icon-only control - exactly the gap a tooltip exists to fill. Don't Required. Must be 8+ characters with a number and a symbol.□ Rules the user needs while typing should not be hidden behind hover - they are invisible on touch and gone the moment the pointer moves. Put them in the field's help text. Accessibility Associated with its trigger via aria-describedby pointing at the tooltip bubble's id, so screen readers announce it as supplementary information about the focused control, not as an unrelated interruption. Appears on keyboard focus, not just mouse hover - the trigger must be focusable (tabindex="0" if it isn't natively) so keyboard-only users get exactly the same hint sighted mouse users do. Deliberately carries no aria-live/role="alert"/role="status": Tooltip is this system's lowest interruption level, a supplementary hint tied to whatever already has focus, not an event that needs to interrupt and announce itself elsewhere on the page. Never the only source of essential information - it must supplement, not replace, a visible accessible name. pages.guide: Component Guide Human View Machine View Overview Tour guides a new user through a sequence of features one at a time - a small card anchored next to a highlighted UI element, with Back/Next navigation and a step counter, used to walk someone through unfamiliar functionality rather than leaving them to discover it alone. When to Use First-time onboarding through key features - a guided walkthrough for new users. A feature-announcement walkthrough - introducing something new to existing users. A multi-step setup guide or contextual help sequence - anchored to the actual UI elements involved. When Not to Use A single, standalone hint about one control - use Tooltip instead of a full multi-step tour. Reference material a user might want to revisit anytime - use static Documentation or a help panel rather than a one-time guided sequence. Frequent or repeated interruptions for returning users - a Tour should typically run once (or be easily dismissed permanently), not repeatedly block the same user. Best Practices Keep the sequence short - a handful of steps at most, focused on genuinely non-obvious functionality. Always let the user skip or exit the tour at any step, not just at the end. Anchor each step precisely to the real UI element it describes, so the highlighted target and the explanation clearly match. Do and Don't Do Step 2 of 3Filters live hereNarrow long lists without leaving the page. A short sequence with the position shown, so the user knows how much is left before they commit. Don't Step 9 of 14This is the Save buttonClick Save to save. Fourteen steps explaining self-evident controls gets dismissed, taking the genuinely useful steps with it. Accessibility Each step's card is exposed as role="dialog" (like Modal, but non-blocking of the rest of the page: aria-modal="false") with an accessible name and description via aria-labelledby/aria-describedby. Focus moves into each step's card as it appears - the same per-step focus management Modal uses on open - so keyboard and screen-reader users follow the same sequence as everyone else, then moves on again as the step advances. Each step is reachable and dismissible by keyboard (Back/Next/Escape), not only by mouse click, and a Skip/Exit control is always keyboard-reachable, not just a small close icon meant for a mouse. The step count and current position ("Step 2 of 4") are exposed as text content read with the step, not conveyed only by a visual progress dot - and no separate aria-live region is used, since each step's arrival is already announced by focus moving to its dialog. pages.guide: Component Guide Human View Machine View Overview Transfer shows two side-by-side list panels with checkboxes, moved between with center arrow buttons - used for choosing a subset of items from a larger pool when seeing both the available and chosen items at once helps the user decide, unlike a multi-select dropdown that hides one side. When to Use Permission or role assignment - moving specific permissions into an assigned list. Building a subset from a larger pool - a playlist builder, a team member picker. Choosing visible columns or tags - column visibility chooser, a tag selector. When Not to Use A single value chosen from a list - use Select - Transfer is for choosing several items, not one. A small option set - a handful of items rarely justifies two full panels; use Checkbox group instead. Hierarchical, nested data - use Tree Select so the structure itself stays visible, rather than flattening it into two plain lists. Best Practices Support search/filter within each panel once the pool of items grows beyond a quick scan. Show a live count of selected items in each panel's header. Keep the moved-to panel's order meaningful (e.g. order added) rather than silently re-sorting it. Accessibility Each row's checkbox is independently focusable and labeled with the item's name. pages.guide: Component Guide Human View Machine View Overview Tree is a standalone, always-visible hierarchical structure with expandable branches - each node can be a folder-like parent with children or a leaf, optionally with a checkbox for multi-select. It's the always-on-page counterpart to Tree Select, which hides the same structure behind a dropdown trigger. When to Use A file or folder browser - nested files and directories the user expands and browses directly. An org chart or category tree - a structure worth keeping visible while the user works, not hidden behind a click. A permission tree with checkboxes - selecting individual nodes or whole branches at once. When Not to Use A form field that picks one value from hierarchical data - use Tree Select so the structure stays hidden until needed, saving space. Linked columns where each choice narrows the next - use Cascader instead of a single expandable tree. Flat, non-hierarchical data - use List or Table; a Tree's indentation and expand controls add nothing when there's no real nesting. Best Practices Keep deeply nested branches collapsed by default, expanding only the path relevant to the current context. Use the Checkable type's parent-checkbox to reflect a partial (indeterminate) selection when only some children are checked. Pair folder/file icons with the indentation, not instead of it - icons alone don't communicate depth as clearly as indentation does. Reach for the Metatext type's second line of supplemental text to disambiguate similarly-named nodes or surface a quick detail (a file size, an item count) without adding a column. Do and Don't Do ▾📁Design📄Icons.fig Folders and files read differently at a glance, and the hierarchy is shown through real indentation, not just a label prefix. Don't Design- Icons.fig A hyphen standing in for indentation collapses the moment there is more than one level deep, and gives folders no toggle to collapse their contents. Accessibility Implemented with tree/treeitem roles, so screen readers announce each node's depth and expanded/collapsed state. Fully keyboard-operable - arrow keys move between nodes, and left/right expand or collapse a branch. Checkbox state (checked/indeterminate/unchecked) is exposed programmatically, not communicated by fill color alone. pages.guide: Component Guide Human View Machine View Overview Tree Select is a select field over hierarchical, nested data - the user picks any node, parent or leaf, at any depth from an indented, expandable tree - used when the option set is too deep or too structured for a flat Select or Cascader's linked columns. When to Use An org chart or folder-structure picker - where any level, not just leaves, is a valid selection. Permission group assignment - picking a specific nested group within a broader hierarchy. A nested tag selector or report hierarchy filter - where the full tree needs to stay visible and explorable at once. When Not to Use A flat, non-nested option list - use Select - a tree adds visual complexity a flat list doesn't need. Data where only leaf nodes are ever valid, and the path itself matters more than seeing the whole tree at once - use Cascader's linked-column drill-down instead. A very large tree with thousands of nodes and no search - add a filter/search mode, or reconsider whether Tree Select is the right control for that scale. Best Practices Let common branches start expanded when the selected value (or a sensible default) lives a level or two deep. Support typing to filter/search across the whole tree once it grows beyond a quick visual scan. Show the selected node's full path in the closed trigger, not just its own label, so the selection stays unambiguous. Do and Don't Do Destination folderDesign / IconsDesignIconsLogos The control shows the whole path, so "Icons" is never confused with another folder of the same name elsewhere in the tree. Don't Destination folderIconsDesignIconsMarketingIcons Showing only the leaf name makes two different folders look like the same choice once the panel is closed. Accessibility Implemented with tree/treeitem semantics, so screen readers announce each node's depth and expanded/collapsed state. Fully keyboard-operable - arrow keys move between nodes, and left/right expand or collapse a branch. The currently selected node is clearly announced, including which ancestor branch it belongs to. pages.guide: Component Guide Human View Machine View Overview Upload adds one or more files to a form - either a large drag-and-drop dropzone or a compact trigger button - paired with a file list that reports each file's name, size, and upload status, so the user always knows what was added and whether it succeeded. When to Use Attaching documents to a record - a support ticket, an application form. Uploading a profile photo or design asset - a single-file, often image-specific upload. Bulk file import - a CSV import, a batch of resumes/CVs. When Not to Use Collecting a URL to an already-hosted file rather than the file itself - use Input or Add-on instead. A field that doesn't actually involve a file - obviously use a different form field type - Upload exists specifically for file transfer. A single, tiny, purely decorative image with no need for status feedback - a simpler custom control may be lighter weight than the full Upload component. Best Practices Always show per-file progress and a clear success/error state, not just a single overall spinner. State accepted file types and size limits up front, before the user picks a file, not only after a rejected upload. Let the user remove a file from the list before final submission, in case they attached the wrong one. Do and Don't Do Drop files or browsePDF or PNG, up to 10 MB eachcontract.pdf2.4 MB Accepted formats and the size ceiling are stated before the user picks a file, and each upload reports its own outcome. Don't Drop files or browsecontract.tiffUpload failed Withholding the rules until after the upload wastes the user's time and bandwidth, and "Upload failed" still does not tell them what to change. Accessibility The dropzone is also operable via a real file-picker trigger, since drag-and-drop alone isn't reachable by keyboard. Upload progress and completion/error status are announced via an aria-live region, not just shown visually. Each file row's remove control is independently labeled with that file's name ("Remove report.pdf"), not a generic "Remove" repeated for every row.
